After completing the series in two weeks, I reached the final stage and implemented the Restaurant Automation Project, then took it a step further by integrating it with the Stock Management Project.

Restaurant Automation — AI-Powered Customer Support & Order Management

The project is a Telegram-based bot that handles customer interactions and automates the restaurant ordering process.

How it works:

🔹Message Classification: An LLM Chain analyzes incoming customer messages and classifies them into three categories: general messages, order requests, and restaurant-related questions.

🔹Specialized Prompts: Each category follows a dedicated prompt to guide the AI Agent in handling the request appropriately.

🔹RAG-Powered Knowledge Base: I integrated a Supabase Vector Store as a knowledge retrieval tool for the AI Agent. Restaurant information, including the menu and other relevant details, is used as a knowledge base to help the agent provide contextual answers grounded in the available information.

🔹Automated Order Processing: When a customer places an order, the agent collects the required customer details, records the order in Orders Sheet, and sends a confirmation message to the customer.

2. Stock Management — Automated Inventory Tracking

also implemented a Telegram-based stock management workflow designed to help restaurant staff track order statuses and manage inventory.

How it works:

🔹 Staff members send the order ID through Telegram along with the corresponding status: Done or Cancel.

🔹 The workflow automatically updates the order status from Pending to Done or Cancel.

🔹 When an order is marked as Done, the workflow extracts each item and its corresponding quantity from the order then automatically deducts the quantities from the inventory.

Integrating Both Workflows was an exciting part to create a more complete automation system.

The Restaurant Automation workflow handles customer interactions and order creation, while the Stock Management workflow supports order status tracking and inventory updates.

- n8n Workflow Automation
- LLM Chains & AI Agents

- Automated Order Processing & Inventory Management

My Weekly Telecom Technology View
26 October 2026

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗔𝗜-𝗥𝗔𝗡 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆 𝗶𝘁.

I’m encouraged by the engineering progress. I’m less convinced by the assumption that putting AI compute into a network automatically creates a business.

This week’s T-Mobile AI-RAN call and Elisa’s trial combining radio and AI workloads move technical feasibility forward. AT&T’s separate AI networking MVP explores another part of the problem: controlling how applications reach models, handle data and consume budget.

There is a bigger telecom story here. The location of computing is becoming part of the service decision.

An industrial application may need inference near a machine. A consumer assistant may keep sensitive processing on the device. Other workloads will run more economically in a central cloud. The operator’s opportunity is to make those choices work together without asking customers to manage the boundaries.

That could change what telcos sell, how they design networks and how they support customers. But first, we need to separate two investment cases: AI that improves radio performance, and AI applications that share network computing resources. 𝗔 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿.

Shared infrastructure introduces a practical tension. Radio processing has deadlines; AI demand can be unpredictable. Protecting connectivity may leave compute idle. Selling that capacity too aggressively could compromise the service customers already pay for.

The commercial design therefore belongs in the architecture discussion. What capacity can be committed? Who pays for reservations? Can the application move elsewhere? Does the price cover power, software, support and partner margins?

I would insist on those answers before approving a wider rollout.

Over time, I see a credible role for telcos in operating distributed AI services. Their reach matters, but the advantage must be earned through reliable delivery, customer access and disciplined economics. Hyperscalers and application providers will remain formidable partners and competitors.

𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗲𝗱𝗴𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝘁𝗼 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗳𝘆 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁?

Most restaurants don’t have a hiring problem. They have a first-week problem. 🔑

We spend time and money recruiting, then hand the new hire an apron, a quick tour, and a “just follow Sam today.”

Then we’re surprised when they leave within the first month.

The first 7 days decide whether someone becomes a committed team member or a statistic. Here’s the simple structure I recommend:

📌 Day 1: Welcome, not survival. Introduce the team, show where everything is, and explain why their role matters. Nobody should spend the first day feeling lost.

📌 Days 2-3: Learn the standards. Show what “good” looks like for the menu, the service steps, and the guest experience. Don’t assume they’ll figure it out.

📌 Days 4-5: Practice with support. Pair them with a strong buddy, not just whoever is available. Let them do real tasks with feedback in the moment.

📌 Days 6-7: Check in. A short, honest conversation: What’s clear? What’s confusing? What do you need from us?

Why does this matter?
✅ Clear expectations reduce stress and early mistakes.
✅ People who feel supported stay longer.
✅ A confident new hire gives better service from the start.
✅ The cost of replacing one employee is far higher than the cost of a good first week.

Great teams aren’t built by finding perfect people. They’re built by giving good people a great start.

The growing use of GLP-1 weight-loss medications.

Medications such as Mounjaro and Wegovy are changing how some consumers approach food, portion sizes, appetite and potentially alcohol consumption.

And that raises an interesting question.

What happens to hospitality when customers still want the experience, but no longer want the quantity?

For decades, much of our industry has focused on generous portions, upselling additional courses, premium drinks packages and encouraging customers to spend more.

🥗 More protein-focused, nutritionally balanced menu choices?

🍸 Greater demand for sophisticated alcohol-free beverages?

🏨 Hotels reconsidering traditional dining packages and buffet offerings?

💷 New approaches to menu engineering, pricing and profitability?

The challenge isn’t simply about serving less food.

It’s about understanding how changing consumer behaviour could influence the entire hospitality experience.

And importantly, smaller appetites don’t necessarily mean smaller expectations.

Customers may still want exceptional service, beautiful surroundings, memorable experiences and outstanding food.

They may simply consume differently.

For operators, this presents both a potential challenge and an opportunity.

The businesses that recognise emerging consumer trends and adapt intelligently could find themselves ahead of the curve.

When building an AI Agent to handle order inquiries, there's one question I need to answer before letting it respond to customers

How does it know which order the customer is actually asking about

Let's say a customer sends a WhatsApp message asking where their order is

They have two open orders and haven't provided an order number

The Agent might understand the question perfectly and still pick the wrong order

It could end up sharing real tracking information from the system, but for a shipment that doesn't belong to that customer

And to me, that's more concerning than the Agent simply not knowing the answer

The customer has no way of knowing the Agent made a guess. They'll assume the information came directly from the system

That's why, if the Agent can't identify the right order, it should ask for the order number or another detail that helps narrow it down

Once it finds the order, it also needs to verify that it actually belongs to the customer before sharing any details

And if there's still uncertainty, it's better to hand the conversation over to a human than keep guessing

This is something I think about when designing AI Agents

Understanding the question isn't enough. There also need to be clear rules for when the Agent can make a decision, when it should ask for more information, and when it needs to stop and involve a human

Because in the end, a fast response isn't what matters most

Getting the right information to the right customer does

Before budgeting your WhatsApp service replies, check which pricing page you are reading.

Two official Meta pages currently tell different stories.

The developer pricing documentation, updated September 30, describes an October 1, 2026 change: each business phone number gets a monthly allowance of 1,000 service messages, with service-message charges starting after that allowance is used. It also describes separate free-entry-point exceptions.

The general WhatsApp Business pricing page still says service replies within the 24-hour customer service window are free.

Those are not interchangeable statements. The service window determines when non-template replies can be sent; it should not be treated as proof that every reply is free under every pricing rule.

This is about the WhatsApp Business Platform/API—not a claim about every message sent from the WhatsApp Business app.

Before changing your budget, ask whoever manages your integration to confirm:

• Which current pricing rules apply to your Messaging account and business phone number.
• Which message categories were actually delivered, rather than merely sent.
• Which deliveries qualified for a free allowance or entry-point exception.
• How the billable deliveries reconcile with the invoice.

I would not turn conflicting documentation into a confident cost forecast. Check the applicable account terms and billing records first.

Does your WhatsApp report distinguish messages sent inside the service window from messages actually marked billable?
